0.title: The Lord, the Giver of Life
0.essay:
Many Christians are confident about God the Father and Jesus the Son, but vague about the Holy Spirit. Some think of him as an impersonal force. Others link him mainly with dramatic experiences, and argue about which gifts are for today. Yet without the Spirit no one would ever be born again, understand the Bible, pray, grow in holiness or persevere to the end.

Better than having Jesus beside you

On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples, “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7). That is an extraordinary statement. The disciples had Jesus with them in person, and he said it was better for them to have the Spirit. The Spirit is not a lesser substitute for Christ. He is Christ’s presence with his people, everywhere and always.

A floodlight

The Spirit’s great work is to glorify Christ. “He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14). He is like a floodlight, which is not meant to be looked at but to make something else visible. Where the Spirit is truly at work, people are not fascinated by the Spirit but by Jesus.

The chapters

Who the Holy Spirit Is; The Spirit Gives Life; The Spirit Within Us; Walking by the Spirit; The Gifts of the Spirit — including which gifts continue today, with the main views and a verdict; and The Spirit, the Word and Mission.

1.title: Who the Holy Spirit Is
1.essay:
Do you think of the Holy Spirit as “it” or “he”? The difference shapes everything. A force is something we try to use; a person is someone we know.

A person

The Spirit is not an energy or a power. Jesus calls him “another Helper” (John 14:16) — another of the same kind as himself. Jesus had been his disciples’ helper for three years; now the Spirit would be, and he would not leave: he would be with them “forever” (John 14:16). The Spirit teaches (John 14:26), speaks (Acts 13:2), intercedes (Romans 8:26), decides (1 Corinthians 12:11) and can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30). Forces do not grieve. Only persons do.

A believer has always prayed, “Lord, send your power,” as though asking for electricity. Learning that the Spirit is a person who loves her, prays for her and can be grieved, she begins to think of him as a constant, gentle companion, and to ask, “Am I grieving him?”

God

Ananias and Sapphira pretended to give the whole price of their land while keeping part. Peter said, “why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit”, and then, “You have not lied to man but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). Lying to the Spirit is lying to God. He is not a force that can be fooled; he is God, who sees the heart.

He has the attributes of God. He is everywhere present (Psalm 139:7), knows the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10–11) and is eternal (Hebrews 9:14). He does the works of God: he was active in creation (Genesis 1:2), inspired Scripture (2 Peter 1:21) and gives new life.

One with the Father and the Son

Jesus told his disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19): one name, three persons. Paul’s blessing joins them in the same way: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14). The Spirit’s particular gift is fellowship: sharing in God’s life and in each other’s.

So he is not a junior partner. He is fully God, equal with the Father and the Son, to be worshipped and glorified with them. Scripture rarely records prayers addressed directly to the Spirit, because his role is to bring us to the Father through the Son. Yet since he is God, it is right to worship him, as the church always has.

Jesus speaks of “the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father”, whom he himself will send (John 15:26). The Western church has confessed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, since he is called both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9).

In the Old Testament

The Spirit did not first appear at Pentecost. He hovered over the waters at creation. He came upon judges, kings and prophets to equip them for their tasks, and gave skill to the craftsmen who built the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3). David prayed, “take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11).

And the prophets promised more. God would pour out his Spirit on all his people (Joel 2:28). Through Ezekiel he promised a heart transplant — a heart of stone replaced by a heart of flesh — and then, “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). What the law could command but not produce, the Spirit would produce from within.

Old Testament believers were made alive by the Spirit too, since no one can be saved without new birth. What is new since Pentecost is the fullness of his work: he is poured out on all believers, not only leaders; he lives in them permanently; and he unites Jew and Gentile in one body.

The forgotten person

When Paul met some disciples in Ephesus, he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit when they believed. They said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit” (Acts 19:2). They had been taught only John’s baptism. Many Christians today are not much further along. They know the Spirit exists, but have little idea who he is or what he does. This study is meant to change that.

For reflection

How would you show from Scripture that the Holy Spirit is a person and not a force? Read John 14:15–26: what does Jesus say the Spirit will do? Why is the Spirit often the “forgotten” person of the Trinity? What difference would it make to pray, read and serve as someone in whom God himself lives?

2.title: The Spirit Gives Life
2.essay:
Nicodemus was a respected teacher of Israel, morally serious and deeply religious. Jesus told him, “unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). Nicodemus did not need improvement. He needed a new beginning, and only the Spirit can give it.

Why new birth is necessary

Nicodemus took Jesus literally and asked how a grown man could be born again. Jesus explained that there are two kinds of birth: “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:5–6).

By nature we are “dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1), and a dead person cannot decide to come alive. “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Before the Spirit works, the gospel seems foolish, unnecessary or unwelcome. Why do some find it compelling and others foolish? Paul’s answer is the Spirit: believers have received him “that we might understand the things freely given us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). That is humbling. If we believe, it is because God opened our eyes.

Water and Spirit

Some take “water” in John 3:5 to mean baptism, so that baptism causes new birth. But Jesus rebukes Nicodemus for not understanding this from the Old Testament (John 3:10). The background is Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and give a new spirit. Water and Spirit together describe the Spirit’s cleansing and renewing work, which baptism later signifies.

Like the wind

“The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). The Spirit is invisible and sovereign. We cannot control or predict his work, but we can see its effects.

He ordinarily works through the word of God (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). As the gospel is heard, he opens blind eyes and gives a new heart. In Philippi, Paul spoke by a river to a group of women, and of Lydia Luke says, “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). Paul spoke the word; the Lord opened her heart. That is how conversion happens. The Spirit does not usually work apart from the word, and the word does not save apart from the Spirit. So we preach the gospel and pray for the Spirit together.

A mother has prayed for years for her adult son, who has heard the gospel many times and shrugs it off. She has tried every argument. Studying John 3, she realises she cannot argue him into new life; only the Spirit can give it. She keeps speaking, but she prays more than she argues.

Life first, then faith

In the Reformed understanding, new birth is not the result of our faith but its cause. God gives life, and the living person believes. That is why salvation is entirely of grace: even our faith is a gift (Ephesians 2:8). The Grace of God study sets out the views on this, with a verdict.

Faith and repentance are the first signs of new life. A new love for God, a new hatred of sin, a new hunger for his word and a new love for his people follow. Paul calls it a washing: “he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (Titus 3:5–6). The whole Trinity is at work, and it is all mercy.

Sealed

When people believe, the Spirit marks them as God’s own. “In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13–14). A seal marks ownership and protects. A guarantee is a down payment, a first instalment that promises the rest. The Spirit in us now is a foretaste of heaven and a pledge that God will finish what he began. God does not make a down payment on something he does not intend to complete.

Can you see signs of new life in yourself: a love for Christ, a hatred of sin, a hunger for God’s word? These are the wind’s effects.

For reflection

Why could Nicodemus’s religion and morality not save him? How does John 3:8 encourage you as you pray for unbelieving friends and family? What does it mean to you that the Spirit is the “guarantee” of your inheritance? What evidence of new life do you see in yourself? Thank God for it.

3.title: The Spirit Within Us
3.essay:
One of the most astonishing truths of the New Testament is that God himself lives in every believer. “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Every believer has the Spirit

In the Old Testament, God’s presence lived in a tent, then a temple. Now he lives in his people. There are not two classes of Christians, those who have the Spirit and those who do not. “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). If you are in Christ, the Spirit is in you, whether you feel it or not.

And he is both a present life and a future promise: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). Our bodies may weaken and die, but the Spirit in them guarantees resurrection.

The Spirit of adoption

“For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). The Spirit turns servants into children. He gives believers the instinct to call God Father, the cry of a child running to a parent. And children are heirs, “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The path to that inheritance runs through suffering with Christ, but it ends in glory with him.

When you pray, do you come as a servant hoping to be accepted, or as a child calling “Father”? The Spirit of adoption makes the second possible.

The Spirit of assurance

“The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16). This witness is not usually a voice or a vision. It is his quiet work of applying God’s promises to our hearts, producing trust, love for God and a growing likeness to Christ, so that we know we belong.

The Spirit who prays

“Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). When grief or confusion leave us silent, the Spirit is praying for us, and always in line with God’s will (Romans 8:27). Even our weakest prayers are carried by a perfect intercessor.

A Christian sits by her husband’s hospital bed, too exhausted and frightened to pray. All she can manage is a sigh. She remembers Romans 8:26. Her silence is not empty; the Spirit is praying for her. She rests in that.

The Spirit who unites

The same Spirit who lives in each believer lives in all believers, binding them into one body: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). That is why Christians from different nations and backgrounds can feel at home with one another at once. The same Spirit lives in both.

Holy ground

Paul wrote about the body as the Spirit’s temple in the middle of warnings about sexual sin. The church in Corinth had serious problems, but Paul did not tell them the Spirit had left. He reminded them that he was there: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The indwelling Spirit makes the body holy ground. His presence is not only a comfort but a reason for holiness.

Is there a second baptism?

Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often describes baptism in the Spirit as a second experience after conversion, usually shown by speaking in tongues, which brings power for service. Others hold that every believer is baptised in the Spirit at conversion, and that later experiences are fillings or renewals of his work, not a second baptism.

The second view is the right one. Paul says “we were all baptized” into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13), and he says it to a mixed and immature church. Baptism in the Spirit is his work of joining us to Christ at conversion. The delays in Acts (Acts 8; Acts 19) mark the gospel crossing new boundaries — Samaria and the Gentile world — under apostolic witness; they are not a pattern for every believer. But the command to “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18) is ongoing. We do not seek a second baptism, but we seek to be filled again and again.

Can the Spirit leave a believer? No. He is given “to be with you forever” (John 14:16). David’s prayer in Psalm 51:11 reflected the Old Testament pattern, in which the Spirit’s anointing for office could be taken away, as it was from Saul.

For reflection

How does it change your view of yourself to know that you are a temple of the Holy Spirit? Read Romans 8:12–27 and list everything the Spirit does for believers. How would you answer a Christian who says they need a second baptism in the Spirit? When have you been unable to pray, and how does Romans 8:26 comfort you?

4.title: Walking by the Spirit
4.essay:
The Christian life is a battle. “For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). Every believer feels this pull in two directions. The answer is not self-improvement but the Spirit: “walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16).

The fruit of the Spirit

Paul sets two lists side by side. The works of the flesh are obvious and destructive. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice that it is fruit, not fruits: one character, the character of Christ, with nine aspects. And it is fruit, not works. Fruit grows. It cannot be manufactured by effort alone, but it can be cultivated by staying close to the vine (John 15:4–5).

Believers “have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5:24), and yet must still “keep in step with the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). The victory was won at the cross, and we live it out day by day.

A man with a quick temper has tried for years to control it with willpower. He begins each day reading Scripture and asking the Spirit to grow patience in him. He still fails sometimes. But his wife notices that he apologises faster and that the outbursts are rarer. The fruit is growing slowly, as fruit does.

Holiness by the Spirit

The Spirit gives the desire and the power to put sin to death: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13). And he changes us gradually into Christ’s likeness. Moses veiled his face after seeing God’s glory; believers now look with unveiled faces, and as they look, they change: “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Transformation comes through beholding. The more we gaze at Christ in Scripture, the more the Spirit makes us like him. Holiness is not instant, but it is real.

Walking by the Spirit does not mean waiting passively. Paul commands effort: put to death, put off, put on, strive. But our effort rests on his work: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

The Spirit and Scripture

The Spirit who inspired the Bible also opens it to us. Jesus had more to teach than his disciples could bear, and he promised that the Spirit “will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13). That promise was first given to the apostles, who wrote the New Testament. But the same Spirit now helps believers understand and believe what was written. This is called illumination. It does not add new truth to Scripture; it helps us see and love what is already there. And notice his aim: “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). Any teaching that exalts experiences of the Spirit above Christ is not from him.

So the Spirit guides believers chiefly through Scripture, wisdom, godly counsel and providence, not through private messages to be obeyed as if they were God’s word. Impressions and feelings should be tested by Scripture and held humbly.

Be filled

“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). Wine controls a person from outside; the Spirit transforms from within. Paul describes what a Spirit-filled life looks like: singing, thankfulness and mutual submission (Ephesians 5:19–21). It is not first an emotional experience but a life increasingly governed by Christ’s word (Colossians 3:16).

The disciples who fled at Jesus’ arrest were the same men who, after Pentecost, stood before the council and refused to stop preaching. The council “recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13). The Spirit had changed fearful men into courageous witnesses.

Do not grieve him

“And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). Paul puts that warning between instructions about speech and anger. The Spirit is grieved not only by dramatic sins but by corrupting talk, bitterness and malice — whatever destroys the unity he creates. Kindness, tenderness and forgiveness please him, because they reflect what God has done for us in Christ (Ephesians 4:32).

Paul also warns, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19). In context it concerns despising God’s word spoken in the church. We quench the Spirit when we resist his word.

Does the Spirit guide our personal decisions?

Should I marry this person? Take this job? Move to that town? And what about the sudden nudge to ring my mother, or the missionary biographies in which someone felt compelled to go to a village, and arrived to find people waiting for a preacher? How does the Spirit lead believers in the ordinary decisions of life?

Two answers Christians give

Some teach that God has a detailed individual plan for every decision, and that the Spirit reveals it through inner impressions, a “sense of peace,” or a quiet voice we must learn to hear. Writers such as Dallas Willard have urged believers to cultivate this kind of listening.

Others, such as Garry Friesen and Kevin DeYoung (Just Do Something), argue that God’s will for us is chiefly his revealed will in Scripture. Within its boundaries we are free to choose wisely, and God is not hiding a secret answer we must decode before we dare act.

What Scripture actually promises

The Reformed view stands much nearer the second answer, while gladly affirming that God is personally involved in every step. The Spirit leads us chiefly in four ways.

Through his word. The Spirit who inspired Scripture now opens our eyes to it and presses it on our consciences. Most decisions are settled here: honesty, purity, faithfulness, love.

Through a renewed mind. “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God” (Romans 12:2). The Spirit does not usually bypass our thinking. He makes it wise. “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5).

Through the church. “In an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14). Even the apostles reached decisions together: “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28).

Through providence. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). God opens and closes doors, and arranges circumstances, often in ways we see only afterwards. John Flavel said providence is like Hebrew: it must be read backwards.

What some favourite verses do not mean

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14) is not about choosing jobs or spouses. The previous verse explains it: being led by the Spirit means putting to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13). The Spirit leads us away from sin. Likewise, “let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15) is about peace between believers in one body, not an inner feeling that confirms a decision. And the dramatic guidance in Acts — Paul forbidden to preach in Asia, then called to Macedonia by a vision (Acts 16:6–10) — came at turning points of the apostolic mission. It is not presented as the normal way every believer decides where to live.

And the nudges?

The Spirit may well use a thought that comes to mind — to pray for a friend, to ring your mother, to speak to a stranger. Those biographies are often true stories of God’s providence. But such impressions are not new revelation and carry no authority of their own. As this app holds, the Spirit no longer gives new revelation alongside Scripture; he works through the word and through his providential care. So test every impression. Does it agree with Scripture? Is it wise? Is it loving? Do mature believers agree? If the nudge is to do something good and harmless, like phoning your mother, simply do it; you needed no special revelation to love her. If it is to make a life-shaping decision, weigh it with Scripture, prayer, counsel and circumstances, and never treat it as “God told me.”

Choosing a spouse

Scripture gives the boundaries: a widow “is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Marry a believer, of godly character, whom you love and who shares your commitment to Christ, with the counsel of those who know you. Within those boundaries, God gives freedom. There is no need to wait for a sign.

Think of a young man torn between two job offers, both honourable. He has prayed for weeks, waiting for a feeling. His pastor asks him: which uses your gifts better, keeps you in a good church, and serves your family? He chooses, trusting God, and later sees God’s kindness in ways he could never have planned. The Spirit was leading all along, through Scripture, wisdom, counsel and providence.

That is freeing. Our security does not rest on reading every impression correctly, but on a Father who “will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go” (Psalm 32:8), and who holds our steps.

For reflection

Read Galatians 5:16–26. Where do you see the flesh and the Spirit in conflict in your life? Why does Paul speak of “fruit” rather than “works”? Which aspect of the fruit is least visible in you? What kind of speech or attitude might be grieving the Spirit in your life?

5.title: The Gifts of the Spirit
5.essay:
The ascended Christ gives gifts to his church through the Spirit. “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Every believer has at least one gift, and every gift is meant to serve others, not to impress them.

Many gifts, one body

The New Testament lists many gifts: teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy, administration, helping, evangelism, faith, wisdom and others (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, 28; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Peter 4:10–11). “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:4); different service, but the same Lord; different activities, but the same God. The Trinity is the pattern of the church: unity without uniformity. And the Spirit distributes gifts “as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). We do not choose our gifts; we receive them.

Paul compares the church to a body. “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). Every member is needed, and the parts that seem weaker are indispensable (1 Corinthians 12:22).

Tools, not trophies

“As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10). Peter divides gifts into two broad groups, speaking and serving. Whoever speaks should speak “as one who speaks oracles of God”; whoever serves should serve “by the strength that God supplies”, “in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). Gifts are given by grace, so no one can boast; they are given to all, so no one can opt out.

Love is greater

Between his two chapters on gifts, Paul places 1 Corinthians 13. The Corinthians were proud of their spectacular gifts but short of love. Tongues without love are “a noisy gong”, and prophetic powers without love are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1–2). Then Paul describes love by what it does: it is patient and kind; it does not envy or boast or insist on its own way. These describe Christ himself, and they are the true sign of the Spirit’s presence.

The church in Corinth was “not lacking in any gift” (1 Corinthians 1:7), yet it was divided, proud and immoral. Spectacular gifts did not make it a spiritual church. The Thessalonians, by contrast, were known for their “work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope” (1 Thessalonians 1:3).

Do the miraculous gifts continue?

Continuationists hold that all the gifts of the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues and healing, continue today. Many read 1 Corinthians 13:10 — “when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away” — as referring to Christ’s return. Some hold an “open but cautious” position.

Cessationists hold that the gifts tied to giving new revelation and confirming the apostles’ message ceased when the apostolic foundation was complete, while the ordinary gifts continue.

The cessationist view is the most faithful to the New Testament’s own shape — and it does not rest on 1 Corinthians 13:10, which most likely does refer to Christ’s return. The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once and then built upon. The miraculous signs confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4) and are called “the signs of a true apostle” (2 Corinthians 12:12). The faith “was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3), and Scripture is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). Prophecy that claims to speak God’s words today would add to Scripture.

That does not mean God has changed. He still does miracles when he chooses, and he heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15). Missionaries have seen remarkable providences. The Spirit is not less active today; cessationism is about the gifts that gave new revelation, not about God’s power. And believers who hold the continuationist view are brothers and sisters, many of them deeply godly.

Finding your gift

Rather than taking long inventories, the best way is usually to serve where there is need, and to listen to what mature believers see in you. Gifts are discovered in use, and faithfulness in small tasks matters more than identifying the perfect role.

A retired man assumes he has no spiritual gift because he cannot preach or lead. But he notices lonely people after the service and phones the sick every week. The elders see what he does not: he has a gift of mercy and encouragement, and the church would be poorer without him.

For reflection

What gifts has God given you, and how do you know? Ask someone who knows you well. Why does Paul put 1 Corinthians 13 between chapters 12 and 14? Summarise the continuationist and cessationist views in your own words. How can you serve someone in your church this week with the gift God has given you?

6.title: The Spirit, the Word and Mission
6.essay:
“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The Spirit is given for mission. His power is not for private enjoyment but for public witness.

Witnesses, not timetables

The disciples had just asked about the timing of the kingdom. Jesus redirected them: the times are the Father’s business; theirs is witness. And the Spirit would give them power for it. The circles of mission widen from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and the rest of Acts follows that map.

Pentecost

Fifty days after Passover, the disciples were gathered in Jerusalem. A sound like a mighty rushing wind filled the house, tongues as of fire rested on each one, and they began to speak in other languages, declaring “the mighty works of God” to pilgrims from every nation (Acts 2:1–11). The signs echo the Old Testament: wind, like the breath that brought the dry bones to life (Ezekiel 37:9–10), and fire, as at Sinai. But now the fire rests not on a mountain but on each believer. And the first thing the Spirit does is give speech. His coming is at once a missionary event.

The tongues at Pentecost were real human languages, understood by the hearers (Acts 2:6–8), a sign that the gospel was for all nations. At Babel, God confused languages and scattered the nations. At Pentecost he began to gather them through the gospel.

Peter, who had denied Jesus before a servant girl, preached to thousands in the same city weeks later, speaking of “this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). The hearers “were cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37), and three thousand were baptised that day. The same man, the same city — but now filled with the Spirit.

Pentecost was a once-for-all event in the history of salvation, like the cross and resurrection. The Spirit was poured out on the church, and he has never been withdrawn. We do not need another Pentecost. We need to rely on the Spirit already given.

He convicts the world

Jesus explained why his leaving was to the disciples’ advantage: the Spirit “will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8). He shows people their sin of unbelief, Christ’s righteousness vindicated by his return to the Father, and the judgment of Satan already passed. We cannot convince anyone of their sin or of Christ’s worth. The Spirit can. That takes the pressure off evangelism. Our job is to speak faithfully; his is to open hearts.

The sword of the Spirit

The Spirit’s chief instrument is the word of God. Paul calls Scripture “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). The Spirit inspired it, illuminates it and uses it to convict and convert. So we must never set the Spirit against the word, as if being “led by the Spirit” meant going beyond Scripture. Where the word is faithfully preached, the Spirit is at work.

Boldness

When the early church faced threats from the authorities, they prayed. They did not ask God to remove the danger; they asked for courage: “grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness” (Acts 4:29). God answered by filling them with the Spirit. The place shook, but the main result was not the shaking. It was that “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31).

Believers who feel timid about sharing their faith should pray for the same thing. Jesus said, “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). We have the Spirit, yet we should pray for more of his work in us, in our churches and in our world.

A shy woman has never spoken to her neighbours about Christ. She begins praying each morning for boldness and for opportunities. A few weeks later, a neighbour mentions a hospital diagnosis. She offers to pray, and finds herself explaining why she trusts God. She did not feel brave. She simply asked, and spoke.

When did you last pray specifically for the Spirit to give you boldness to speak about Christ?

For reflection

Read Acts 2:1–41. What does the Spirit do, and what is the result? How does John 16:8 take pressure off you in sharing your faith? Why is it dangerous to set being “led by the Spirit” against Scripture? Who do you long to hear the gospel? Pray for boldness, and for the Spirit to open their heart.
